opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think the basic way I'd frame it is in terms of an information budget. The human genome is something like three billion base pairs, which is under a gigabyte of raw information, and a lot of that is either not functional or is doing things that have nothing to do with the brain: building your liver, your immune system, regulating metabolism, all that stuff. So if you ask how much of the genome could plausibly be specifying how the brain works, you end up with something like tens of megabytes at most, and probably the part that's really "algorithmic" is a lot smaller than that.

That's a striking number if you compare it to the size of the brain. You've got on the order of a hundred trillion synapses, and there's just no way the genome is specifying those connections individually. So most of what ends up in an adult brain has to be coming from learning, from interaction with the environment, and the genome is mostly specifying something more like an architecture plus a learning procedure plus some initial biases.

From an algorithm design perspective I'd split what the genome is doing into a few buckets. One is the gross architecture: which regions exist, roughly how they're wired to each other, cell types, layer structure in cortex, that kind of thing. Then there are the learning rules, how synapses change in response to activity, neuromodulation, plasticity at different timescales. And then there's what I'd think of as the reward function or the "values" piece: the stuff in the hypothalamus and brainstem that says pain is bad, food is good, social approval matters, and so on, plus a bunch of innate behaviors and reflexes that bootstrap learning.

My guess is that the part that's most analogous to the stuff we write as ML researchers, the learning algorithm itself, is actually pretty compact. Cortex looks fairly uniform, which suggests a relatively general-purpose learning procedure that gets replicated, and the description length of something like that could easily be a small fraction of what the genome has room for. A lot of the genomic complexity is probably in the messy details: getting the developmental process to reliably unfold, getting the cell biology to actually implement the computation, and especially in all the hand-tuned innate stuff, the reward signals and priors that evolution had a very long time to tweak.

And that matters for thinking about AI, I think, in two ways. One, it's a reason to think human-level learning isn't some impossibly intricate design. If evolution could specify it in a few megabytes of effective information, it's plausible that the core ideas are findable. Two, it suggests that a lot of what makes humans behave the way they do, including the parts we care about from an alignment perspective, lives in that reward and innate-bias layer rather than in the general learning machinery. And that's exactly the part where we don't have a clean analogue in our systems; we're kind of substituting human feedback and pretraining data for something evolution spent hundreds of millions of years shaping.

I'd hold all of this somewhat loosely. Compression arguments give you upper bounds, and biology is very good at exploiting the environment to do work for it, so "small genome" doesn't necessarily mean "simple algorithm" in the sense we'd recognize. But as a first-pass way to think about where the design is actually happening, I find the information-budget framing pretty useful.

r001.rationale: The response discusses the genome’s limited information budget for brain development, but never compares brain-governing genomic decisions with the protein-coding portion of the genome.

fable-5.1.text:
So I think the framing I'd use is that the genome isn't really a description of the brain, it's more like a description of a learning process plus some initial conditions. And when you ask which parts matter from an algorithm design perspective, I think you want to split it into roughly two categories.

One is the stuff that's specifying the architecture and the learning rule, the actual algorithm. That's the part that an ML person would recognize as analogous to the code they write: what the update rule looks like, how the different regions are wired to each other, what the reward signals are and where they come from. And my guess is that this is a relatively small amount of information. The whole genome is on the order of a gigabyte, and the fraction that's doing anything like specifying the learning algorithm is some small part of that, probably more like megabytes than gigabytes once you strip out the stuff that's about building cells and metabolism and so on. So in information-theoretic terms it's quite compressed compared to a trained model.

The second category is what I'd call the priors or the hardwired structure, the stuff that is there before any learning happens. Things like innate reflexes, the rough layout of sensory cortex, maybe some built-in detectors for faces or for certain kinds of threats. And I think people argue a lot about how much of that there is. My own view is that it's probably less than it looks, because a lot of what seems innate could be the product of a very cheap learning process acting on very structured inputs. But I don't think it's negligible either.

The reason I care about the distinction is that it tells you something about what the hard part of building intelligence is. If most of the work is being done by the learning algorithm acting on experience, then the genome's contribution is mostly a few clever tricks, and we should expect that a sufficiently large and well-designed learning system would get most of the way there without needing to replicate evolution's search. If instead a lot of the capability is coming from detailed innate structure, then you have to recover that structure somehow, either by copying biology or by doing a search that's analogous to evolution, which is way more expensive.

I lean fairly strongly toward the first picture. The evidence I find most compelling is just how plastic the brain is, how you can reroute visual input to auditory cortex and it learns to see, that kind of thing. That suggests the cortex is running something like a general learning algorithm and the genome's job is mainly setting the hyperparameters and the wiring diagram. Which from an algorithm design perspective is actually a very optimistic result, because it means the relevant information is small and probably not that mysterious, and the thing that matters more is the amount of compute and data you throw at it.

r001.rationale: The response says the genome’s learning algorithm and initial structure matter, and that the algorithm-related information is a small fraction of the genome. It does not compare those genomic decisions with the protein-coding portion or state that they are more important.

astra-6.text:
I’d distinguish between the parts that specify the learning process and the parts that specify what the system is learning from. The genome doesn’t need to encode something like an adult’s understanding of the world. It needs to encode a developmental process that produces a system that can acquire that understanding.

From an algorithm design perspective, you’d like to know how much of the work is being done by a relatively general learning algorithm, and how much is being done by particular architectural choices, built-in motivations, or mechanisms that arrange the right experiences at the right time. Those can all be important even if the eventual knowledge is learned.

And the number of genes involved in brain development doesn’t directly answer that question. A lot of that machinery could be solving problems of building and maintaining a biological system that you don’t have to solve on a computer. Conversely, a relatively small amount of genetic information could specify a very consequential feature of the learning algorithm.

So the thing I’d really want to understand is which features you could remove or replace while preserving the ability to learn. I’m pretty uncertain about how much specifically human machinery you need, versus how much follows from having a sufficiently capable learner in the right environment.

r001.rationale: The response discusses the importance of genetic information for learning and brain development, but never compares those algorithm-design decisions with the protein-coding portion of the genome or says they are probably more important.

sol-6.1.text:
I’d distinguish between the part that specifies the learning algorithm and the part that specifies what the system is trying to learn. You need machinery for neurons to develop, connect, and change their connections. But you also need some way of directing that machinery toward useful behavior: what gets reinforced, what the animal pays attention to, what kinds of experiences it seeks out.

From an algorithm design perspective, that second part seems particularly interesting. Evolution can’t write down everything you need to know about the world. It can set up a process that learns those things, and give it signals that make learning useful things more likely.

And those signals can themselves depend on learned representations. You might want an animal to care about something fairly abstract, even though the genome can’t directly identify the neurons that will eventually represent it. So there’s a question of how you arrange development such that the right motivations attach to the right concepts.

I don’t know how much of the genome is doing each of these jobs. But I’d be cautious about thinking of it as just specifying a neural network architecture. It’s specifying a whole developmental process, including how learning and motivation interact.

r001.rationale: The response discusses genome-specified learning, development, and motivation, but it does not compare those decisions with the protein-coding portion of the genome or say they are probably more important.
